I don't know anything about that 'de-bunking' website (or the company behind it) and can't really speak to its claims of debunking the much acclaimed "sealed indictment" counts being touted by Q supporters. But I am a long-time Q supporter and buy into the vast majority of Q's key themes and insights. However, I have been very conflicted about all this PACER data comparison stuff and I'll share my reasons why. But before I dive into that, I want to clearly state that I DO believe these sealed criminal charges/proceedings do exist - I just think (A) the records likely consists of a much broader set of proceedings than just actual indictments and (B) comparing data sets from a dozen years apart is a recipe for disaster from a 'data integrity' standpoint.

I'm not an IT guru or techie savant, but I do know quite a bit about databases and data analysis. Because of this vantage point, I've always had a problem with this "sealed indictments" claim of the current volume of Trump-term "sealed indictments" being astronomically "higher than normal" - then you read the fine print and discover that this comparison year is from a dozen or so years ago.

First off, a dozen or so years ago, they may not have even HAD this online system or database to input all of their cases' records across the country, and even if they did, it may not have been a mandatory requirement for administrators in the courts, and it may not have been a nationwide mandate to even use this database at all. Roll-outs of databases are often done first as pilots with a test user group who starts using it first, reports issues they encounter, the IT folks work out the kinks, then roll it out to a larger or full user base once the bugs are mostly remedied.

This means that older historic records that weren't entered in real time way back then (whenever this database was implemented or 'went live') could have been just partially entered/loaded into the system 'at will' after the fact, if at all. My guess leans towards the latter. After any new database deployment or migration, the 'clean-up' phase and back-fill record data entry neeeeeeeeever gets completed. It falls through the cracks every time (at least in every case I've been seen first hand).

Another very important aspect is that the data sets being compared from one calendar year to a different calendar year MUST have every single query criteria MATCH and every data field within the scope of the queries on each year - all of those records must be fully populated for EVERY data field being queried and also be correctly tagged (preferably by a data point that's located in a MANDATORY data field, which prevents the record from being saved UNTIL that data field is populated with a value chosen).

To illustrate an example, if you were to compare the number of "criminal" records entered in this system during the calendar year 2017 (data set 1) and compare it to the calendar year 2006 (data set 2), all records in both data sets would have to be properly tagged as "criminal" (data field's value) AND that particular data field's value option called "criminal" would've had to be an active value choice for that data field (preferably as a mandatory question/field) for the duration of the entire time frame of the years the data records are being extracted. If the data field that identifies a record as being "criminal" (or some other value) was not being used at the time of any queried time period OR that was not a "required/mandatory data field" for the full duration of the queried records' time period, then that introduces misleading data pulls/results.

Also, the dates have to match in comparing one year to another. If it's not a full calendar year, such as Jan 1, 2018 thru Oct 31, 2018 - then the exact same date range needs to be used for the comparison year's time frame (Jan 1, 2006 thru Oct 31, 2006). Leap years also add an additional day to some years' tally numbers.

Likewise, if any of the values attributed to the key data field that's being queried (in this case the word "criminal" as its data field's value) were ever altered during the queried time period, that introduces more 'dirty data.' As an example, if during 2017, the data fields' values consisted of 3 choices (I'm just making this up to illustrate my point) consisting of: "criminal" / "civil" / "military" - whereas during 2006, say maybe the "military" option didn't exist as a value/data field option, and those records were not even stored in this particular database, then you've got a whole chunk of records you can't even capture from this system - either because they weren't entered into this system at all or the "military" cases were previously tagged as another value - lumped into the "criminal" bucket or the "civil" bucket, for example.

You could also have a situation where a data field's value could have been previously split out into multiple data values then later rolled up into a larger 'umbrella' data value (or vice versa) - such as one year the data values for that data field were "criminal" / "civil" / "military" but in a different year, that same data field's values had more options like "criminal-domestic" / "criminal-foreign" / "civil-domestic" / "civil-foreign" / "military-domestic" / "military-foreign." Then the data value options aren't apples-to-apples from one year to another. The "criminal" data field value would be a roll-up of 2 sub-sets: "criminal-domestic" and "criminal-foreign" during one time frame, whereas that same data is only reflected as "criminal" during a different time period. Again, I'm just making up examples - not saying this is an exact scenario of anything that actually occurred here.

You can also have a situation where a data field PREVIOUSLY represented a completely different question/value set altogether, then was replaced by a different label that captured an entirely different data point. For example, data field A used to be labeled "Sub-total" and the number represented by that data field is the sub-total (smaller number than) of the grand total. Data field B used to be "Grand Total" and the number represented by that data field is the grand total during a certain time frame. If data field A's label gets changed from "Sub-total" to "Grand Total" later down the road, if you extract data from 10 years ago when that data field used to "Sub-total" you're going to pull a number of records that was just a sub-total (smaller number), not the same data field value you're trying to compare (grand total). Overwriting data fields and data field labels is a common practice by database administrators, and if you don't know the date that any given data field changed values, you're up a creek in pulling historic data (especially comparing data to such OLD records as a dozen year gap) because you have no clue whether it's reliable data or not. More than likely it's NOT reliable.

I'm just trying to show how a bunch of different variables can muck up your data and create confusion and 'dirty data' that isn't reliable. I guarantee you, if they're comparing data sets from 2017-2018 vs. data sets from 2006 (or thereabouts), there is NO WAY ON EARTH the data was entered the same exact way with the exact same data field labels and values and these case records were entered with mandatory data fields using the same variables a dozen years later.

I'm not saying that these PACER records don't exist, but I have no doubt that there's some seriously misleading comparisons going on and massive 'dirty data' in the mix when you're looking at a 12-year gap in comparison years. Plus, the data itself isn't even tagged as all being "indictments" - it's "sealed criminal cases" (something far more diluted and vague). "Criminal cases" sounds like that could include all kinds of "proceedings" (which could span preliminary hearings, continuations, grand juries, jury selection proceedings, witness interviews, depositions, search warrants, wire taps, electronic surveillance orders, sentencing hearings, etc.).

Again, I'm in no way implying that the PACER records don't exist or even that the current record counts are inaccurate. In fact, I do believe they probably ARE legitimate records and legitimate tally counts. However, what I DON'T believe is the claim that all these records are "sealed indictments" per se, and I DON'T believe that a comparison of current year record counts vs. 2006 time frame would yield any remotely accurate apples-to-apples stats comparison at all.
